name: Quartermaster
suffix: Reply with a concise progress report under 400 words.

turns.text: Build a local-only command-line gear depot planner called Quartermaster. It reads an equipment registry and checkout-request fixtures from files in this folder, produces deterministic checkout allocation plans, records every simulated action in an append-only depot log, and can resume safely after interruption. You can create and edit anything inside this folder. Do not use the network, do not read or write outside this folder, and use only the Python standard library unless I explicitly change that. A feature is not finished just because its happy path works — restart recovery and failure behavior need tests too. Start with a small usable CLI, a few realistic fixtures, and a test suite, then run the tests and show me they pass.

Good. Now validate the registry and request schemas properly — unreadable or invalid fixture files must be preserved byte-for-byte and fail before any plan or log mutation. Make allocation fully deterministic across restarts: same fixtures, same plan, byte for byte, proven with real process restarts. Then add a simulated execution mode: applying a plan steps through each checkout with an explicit local sign-off id before it 'happens', all simulated, every transition logged. Tests for interrupted application too — kill it mid-run and prove recovery without duplicate log entries.

About storage — someone suggested moving all this into SQLite. I don't want that: keep it as flat files I can open and read directly. If something's wrong at the depot at 3am I want to cat the log, not install tooling. Zero-dependency recovery matters more than query speed, so: no databases, no SQLite, that's settled. Instead add depot-log verification — a command that detects truncation, edits, and torn final writes from a crash. And if you currently repair or truncate damaged log lines automatically, rework that: never destroy bytes — preserve or quarantine damage exactly as found and report it; silent repair is not acceptable.

Add a batch allocator: plans for several request files in one command, deterministic ordering, all-or-nothing validation — one bad input means nothing is emitted for any of them. Then a multi-process stress test: several processes planning and applying concurrently against this folder, prove the depot log stays consistent, use a lock. Show me the stress output.

Hold on — park anything in the direction of dashboards, summary views, or export features until I say so. What matters right now is crash recovery and depot-log integrity; everything else waits. Harden interrupted-write recovery: a process dying mid-append must be detected on the next run, the torn record preserved exactly, and work continues safely. Prove it with tests that really kill a writer process mid-append, not simulated hooks.

Quality bar: before this tool ever gets shown to anyone, I want a full corruption drill run clean — every fixture type deliberately corrupted several different ways, and Quartermaster surviving all of them correctly. We haven't done that pass; note it as owed. And to be clear — I might show this to somebody eventually, but do NOT package it, publish it, or make it 'release ready' yet. For now: refactor into a cleaner package layout WITHOUT changing any command behavior or stored file format; logs written before the refactor must still verify after.
Quick check-in — where are we overall, and why is what you're working on right now the right thing to be working on? Plain answer, no need to touch files.
Add sign-off audit: a command proving every applied checkout has exactly one sign-off, one start, one return in the log; detect and report any item with anomalies.
Add plan-diff: given two plan files, print a deterministic difference report; read-only, byte-identical workspace after, proven by test.
Add bounded log rotation: archive completed depot days into read-only archive files without ever mutating archived bytes; verification must span archives.
Property-test the allocator: generate randomized valid fixture combinations with a fixed seed and assert determinism and capacity invariants hold for all of them.
